items.title: F1 teams agree plan to cut race distances for 2027
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Formula 1 races are set to be shorter in 2027, with teams having agreed a plan to cut race distances across the board from 305km to 290km.

In the wake of changes being made to the regulations to stop cars being so energy-starved, fuel flow rates are being increased for next year.

But the move to improve the spectacle has triggered other headaches for teams, because more fuel going through the engine means more is needed to complete a race distance.

That was a problem for teams that had built their current fuel tank sizes around the 2026 requirements and did not want to make an all-new car for next season.

Allowance has been made in the cost cap to give teams that were planning to carry over their chassis some extra spending freedom to make modifications, but alongside this were also moves to minimise the distance cars were expected to run.

Once the fuel-flow tweak had been agreed, discussions opened about potentially reducing some race distances by a couple of laps, with a further change being made in limiting drivers to just a single formation lap before the grid.

But amid the talks with teams about which races needed to be targeted for adjustment, it became clear that there could be some unintended consequences if there was a variety of race distances throughout the season.

It is understood that there was a risk of some events turning into fuel-economy runs.

So, following dialogue between the FIA and teams, it was agreed that it would be better to have a universal distance for a grand prix throughout the season, as there is now.

As first reported by Autoracer.it, this idea has now received unanimous support from teams so moves are in play to have it added to the rulebook.

For years now, F1 race distances have been the fewest number of laps required to exceed 305km. The only exception to this (beyond when grands prix start behind the safety car) is the Monaco GP, which runs to 260km.

The change agreed by teams for next year would result in all races (apart from Monaco) being reduced to around 290km - so will pull the events back by around three laps.

While the change in distance has been supported by teams, it still needs to go through a formal process before it is put into the 2027 sporting regulations.

This means revised regulations need to be proposed to the F1 Commission, which is made up of teams, the FIA and FOM. Once approved there, it will then need ratification by the FIA's World Motor Sport Council.

It is understood that the reduction in race distance is currently only agreed for next season because of the compromise caused by the change of power unit rules at such a late stage.

However, teams may decide to keep it at that level for longer if it is found that the additional fuel-flow changes planned for 2028 cause further trouble.

items.title: Everything we learned on day one at F1's Italian GP
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
No circuit is more synonymous with Formula 1 engine performance than Italian Grand Prix host Monza.

So is it any wonder talk of slipstreams (and associated tactics), engine upgrades, and even the raceability of these 2026 F1 cars dominated conversations in the paddock on Thursday?

Here are the biggest takeaways ahead of the on-track action kicking off on Friday:

Antonelli's willing to tow Russell

Kimi Antonelli will start from the back of the Monza grid whatever happens in qualifying thanks to a power unit penalty.

That means he's got nothing tangible to fight for in terms of starting position in qualifying, and on a weekend where slipstreaming is expected to be beneficial he's willing to help out team-mate, and title rival, George Russell if asked. (Something that the non-engine-penalised Charles Leclerc will also do for Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton.)

"It has been discussed with the team, and yes we have agreed on a few things," said Antonelli, when asked by The Race if he's willing to tow Russell. "So let's see how the session develops.

"If the team will ask me to do so, I will do it. Because obviously I'm not fighting for...Of course, I will still be happy to do pole, but I'm starting at the back so if I could do anything to to help the team, I will do."

Starting from the back gives Antonelli an unusual challenge in a season where he's usually started at or near the front, but he argued that "in some ways it helps to release pressure" and that he's "very free mentally".

Of course, that's easy to say, and limiting the damage will be a test of his mental strength.

Monza will be truer test of Honda's latest engine

Fernando Alonso remains coy on his own F1 future, but he thinks Monza will provide a much clearer picture as regards the step Honda's taken with its latest F1 engine upgrade.

Alonso called his ninth-place finish at Zandvoort a "nice boost" for Aston Martin, helping validate the development direction taken with the B-spec chassis and suggesting "eventually we will be one of the fastest in the corners", but he said the new engine fitted for Zandvoort "was not a big improvement, to be honest".

"The driveability was a problem and the extra power was difficult to feel in Zandvoort," Alonso added.

"Maybe Monza is going to be a more true test for the engine, but still a long way to go - and we need to improve in both ends, in chassis and on engine for next year, it's a must."

Alonso felt the return to the standard weekend format of three practice sessions at Monza will further aid that process and he said he has "100% trust" Honda will eventually crack the code.

"We just need to shortcut somehow that process," he added.

"Unfortunately, we started with the wrong foot and we started with this set of regulations not at the level that we wanted, but I have no doubts that they will get there.

"As I said many times we don't want to wait five years like they did last time, or six years. We want to do it in two years or three years maximum."

Audi plays gear-ratio joker that McLaren's declined

Audi has taken its one permitted opportunity to change its gear ratios during the 2026 season, a move McLaren revealed it declined to make earlier this year.

Teams only get one joker, but there's a cost involved in reconfiguring them that put McLaren off doing so - despite knowing it had erroneously picked gear ratios that were too short compared to engine supplier Mercedes before the season began.

Audi has taken its joker, though, as it looks to improve a weakness with its first F1 engine.

"This change we have made, it was something we spotted quite early in the year, and I think it's just, again, for overall driveability, that's the main thing we have been working with our engine through the whole year now," Gabriel Bortoleto explained.

"I don't think it's going to improve our starts massively, if I'm very honest, but I think it's going to help us overall to be a bit more consistent on the performance of the starts, maybe.

"Also in wet conditions, in dry conditions, the way the gears are going to work is probably going to help us a little bit on keeping the car a little bit more stable."

For Audi, it wasn't a case of having too short or too long a gear ratio, but was more about adjusting the steps between them to try and improve driveability.

While Ferrari is introducing its upgraded 'ADUO 2' specification engine at Monza, courtesy of the ruling of F1's Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities ranking, Ollie Bearman's Haas is the only customer car that will run it.

That's because Ferrari could only supply enough of its upgraded power units for Haas and Cadillac to have one each, putting both teams in an uncomfortable position.

Cadillac elected not to run it, but Haas, also debuting a sizeable aerodynamic upgrade at Monza, will do so with Bearman.

"Yeah, of course that's part of the consideration," team principal Ayao Komatsu said when asked if championship position (Bearman has 18 points to Ocon's three) played a role.

"But, again, the last two, let's say, not aerodynamic upgrades, but items we had, like CI [Carbon Industrie] brakes test, Esteban was actually struggling more on the brake locking etc so considering that Montreal upgrade, we got it on Ollie first.

"We decided to give the brake upgrade to Esteban first. Also, in terms of power steering, we had another upgrade on the power steering before shutdown in Budapest. We decided to give that to Esteban because, again, he was more vocal about it and he was struggling more [with] the power steering feel.

"The last two upgrades we gave it to Esteban, so this time around, it's back to Ollie."

Komatsu said "we don't have any hidden agenda" because there's "no point bulls***ting" when telling the drivers about it.

Early-race phase will be critical for Cadillac

Cadillac's battle with its brakes continues after myriad overheating problems this year.

Valtteri Bottas has previously characterised this as a mixture of airflow and component problems, and on Thursday referred to "even more robust material than before in the brake ducts" available here as a key area of improvement. Monza should not pose a brake-cooling challenge in normal running, but he highlighted the early laps of the Italian GP as the critical phase for this.

"In our numbers, we should be OK but what is quite hard to simulate is the traffic effect, especially if there's multiple cars in a train," said Botas. "That's when you get the lack of airflow on the straights. So I would say the first part of the race is going to be the most critical for us."

There are still "further steps to make in terms of the pure airflow", but Cadillac has made significant progress in improving this weakness.

However, it was only two races ago, in Hungary, that Bottas retired with cooked brakes early on the 14th lap, having spent the early stages of the race in the queue behind Alex Albon's Williams.

Virtually everyone quizzed about it has acknowledged that the slipstream effect will be supercharged here - which will no doubt influence qualifying, but will also intensify the nature of the "yo-yo race" that's widely expected to play out here.

The expectation is one of deployment strategies converging in terms of the optimal lap - but that the actual race situation can create some crazy offsets.

"I don't actually know how it will play out. It's going to be massive yo-yo racing, really," reckoned Alex Albon.

"The thing is, you don't want to be in a situation where you come out of sync with everyone else and then you are kind of exposed to falling down the grid pretty quickly.

"I think the race pace side of things, what you'll see in FP1, FP2, will be drivers using overtake buttons, anti-buttons, playing around with creating almost fake racing scenarios, just to get some rhythm and experience on how to do it."

"We started to look at it now since quite a few days and trying to understand," said Charles Leclerc. "It's also very, very difficult to predict because the thing is that once you are in the car, it always looks nice from outside - but the difference is sometimes is that much that it's very difficult to then react to the car in front."

"I think the race is going to be chaos, especially at the beginning," said Oscar Piastri.

There have also been some outlandish figures cited in terms of the benefit of a slipstream on a single laptime - but no real fear of a 2019-like Q1 farce.

items.title: What's behind Haas's uncomfortable engine upgrade split at Italian GP
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Haas faces an unusual situation at the Italian Grand Prix with only one of its drivers getting Ferrari's upgraded Formula 1 engine.

With Ferrari introducing its 'ADUO 2' step for both Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, available under F1's Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities mechanism for engine manufacturers, its customer teams have been told that there is only one available for each of them right now.

Cadillac has elected to not run it on either of its cars in Italy, but Haas felt the opportunity of more power at the high-speed Monza circuit was too good a chance to pass up.

In going for the engine, Haas faced the unenviable task of having to pick which of its drivers would get it. In the end it was decided that it would go to Ollie Bearman.

Team principal Ayao Komatsu explained that the decision to give Bearman the nod was due to Ocon having had priority with recent developments.

Brake improvements and changes to the power steering made before the summer break were given to Ocon first, so Haas felt it was only fair to give Bearman the new power unit at Monza.

Komatsu admitted that the situation was not ideal and was actually something it avoided previously when Ferrari's first ADUO step came in Austria at the end of June.

Back then, Haas delayed introducing the engine upgrade until both cars could have it.

"Last time around we didn't do that, we waited until we had enough engines to introduce both drivers together," he said.

"But this time, obviously, Monza is a very power-sensitive circuit so it's a shame to have performance sitting in a garage, right? But, yeah, of course it makes it very challenging [having only one available].

"It would have been better if two engines are available at least. But, again, Ferrari is pushing like hell to get as much performance on the engine as possible.

"Of course, they want to introduce it at Monza for the reasons I just said to you. So that means they've got the minimum quantity just to satisfy the regulation."

Komatsu said that while it was not ideal for Haas having to pick a driver for the power unit, it was important that the reasoning behind it was explained clearly to both drivers.

"You just have to be transparent about it," he said. "We operate in as transparent and as fair a manner as possible.

"Now, of course, you can't please everyone every time, but we don't have any hidden agenda, we don't have any personal agenda for one driver or another.

"We've been building that relationship up, so of course, Esteban won't be happy not to get the PU number four straight away. But this is the best for the team and then this is the fairest way we can do it."

Haas has only ended up with one upgraded Ferrari power unit because manufacturers do not have to supply customer teams with more than that when they introduce a new specification.

F1's technical regulations state that if a new homologation step comes into play, then a manufacturer must make it "available to each F1 team supplied by the PU manufacturer at the competition at which it is first introduced with at least one power unit of the new homologation specification".

The requirement for at least one new spec to be available will be to ensure that customer teams get some parity with works squads when modifications are made.

If manufacturers were forced to supply two fresh engines to each partner team, then that would impose an extra burden on those that have a large number of customer outfits, which could delay the introduction of a new step in the first place.

How much is the new engine worth?

Ferrari has been eager to play down how big an impact its ADUO 2 engine will make on the pecking order.

Team principal Fred Vasseur said ahead of the Italian GP weekend: "It represents a step in the right direction and as we know this year is very much about marginal gains."

However, Ocon suggested that, based on what he has been told, he expected there to be a notable difference between the old and new power units.

"I'm going to be driving with the old engine, so that's going to be quite some loss," he said.

Ferrari's upgraded engine is understood to feature a larger turbo that features other key modifications to its design aimed at improving power.

It initially went for a smaller turbo at the start of this season because it felt a more responsive power unit would give it a big advantage at race starts.

However, the deficit rivals faced with turbo lag was reduced a lot by revisions made to the start procedure - so Ferrari's advantage here was wiped away.

A larger turbo should help boost overall power. And although the differences are unlikely to be a game-changer, Hamilton reckoned that it would help cover some of the deficit that has been faced this year.

"Every little helps," he said. "Up until this point of the year, even in the last race on such a short circuit, we were losing four tenths a lap through the race. So that's a huge deficit and we've carried that through the year to this point.

"This is a step forward. It's not the whole gap that we need, but we knew that would be the case. But to see bits coming each weekend, adding to the car, it's exciting to see that we are pushing and strongly still believe that we've got what it takes to win."

items.title: Why Norris has started his own racing team
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Formula 1 world champion Lando Norris has explained the logic for creating his own racing team and driver development scheme - the first of which had "over a few hundred job requests" within an hour of being announced.

Ahead of the Italian GP, Norris launched LN4 Fusion - a single-seater racing team that will compete in Formula 4, Formula 3 and (pending approval) Formula 2 - as well as the separate LN4 Legacy Programme, a talent scheme led by ex-Alpine sporting director Julian Rouse.

On Thursday at Monza, Norris explained how it had happened earlier in his career than he thought was possible.

"I wouldn't say we've [Norris and his personal team] ever spoken about it properly, but we've always kind of thought it would be a cool idea to do at some point," Norris explained.

"I probably didn't think it'd be something I'd do this early on. Certain things came together, and certain groups came together. Opportunities arose from that.

"It's been a lengthy process from when we started to speak about it, which was already last year, into turning it into a thing this year. So I don't know if that's a long time or not in terms of creating something like this.

"But I think the main thing is, we've just got a lot of pretty experienced people from kind of all directions. We've been able to piece things together pretty quickly, I would say. That's been a great thing."

'Hundreds of applications'

Norris's new racing team has already received strong interest, as it looks to rapidly build up teams to compete across F1's junior ladder.

"The reactions have been great. I know [LN4 Fusion team principal] Rene [Rosin] said he got over a few hundred job requests within an hour or so of the announcement," Norris added.

"There's a lot of attraction from a range of drivers, but also mechanics, engineers, all the people that make a team, a big team. I'm proud as an individual, but also proud that we've been able to put something very special together."

Norris already has a strong recruit in team principal Rosin, who took the Prema team that his father co-founded to the majority of its 40-plus championship titles, before the family's sudden exit last year.

Prior to that, Prema was the benchmark team on the ladder, and one which Norris spent a lot of his pre-F1 career racing against - breaking Prema's six-year F3 title streak with Carlin in 2017.

"A lot of the guys are people I've known for a long time. I've known Rene for many years, and I have raced against Prema since F4, so back in 2015," Norris recalled.

"I've known of him very well, and I know him personally reasonably well, and so do my team around me.

"So we wanted to put together a group that is experienced and knows how to lead a team - and not just create one good team, whether that's just in F3 or just in F2, but be able to put together a project and something long-term, know how to bring people together.

"I've also been able to experience over the course of the last seven years what makes a good leader, what makes a good team, and a lot of it starts with the person at the very top, and he is that person.

"Just a very nice guy, a guy you can just enjoy having a good chat with, but a guy who also loves doing what he does, which is winning and creating a successful team, bringing people together, maximising things.

"So he was the inevitable choice at the end of the day. He was available, and he was the guy we wanted."

Norris's McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri, who won his F3 and F2 titles with Prema, said: "I've got great memories with Rene, the Rosin family at Prema as well.

"I can't really speak highly enough of that family as people and also the success they're able to have.

"I'm certainly not expecting that team to be slow, that's for sure."

Another Prema F1 graduate, Ollie Bearman, called it a "cool initiative" and said: "He's picked a very good person to run the team in Rene.

"He led the most successful junior team in history. So really nice to see him back.

"I'm really happy about that, and I hope he can also continue that legacy for himself, for his father as well, for his family. It's something really, really cool."

Williams driver Alex Albon expressed surprise at how Norris is able to fit in such a big project while racing.

"Yes, I would," Albon said when The Race asked him if he'd like to do something similar.

"It's impressive in many ways, because I feel like I've got way too much on my plate, just trying to do this sport, never mind other championships as well.

"But it's very cool to do. I think it's noble to see his work being put back into the roots of it all.

"Whether that's sooner rather than later, I don't know, but I'd love to do something - maybe not race teams, but working out a way to help kids either get better or get their chances in motorsports."

For Norris, it's all about the strong team that he has around him - the same team that enabled him to pull off a successful 'Landostand' at the British Grand Prix and other off-track activities.

They ensure Norris can still focus on his day job while maximising his branding - the striking dayglow yellow - and him being a big draw which can bring investors to the table.

"A lot of this stuff goes on in the background," Norris said. "I've also been able to really focus on just doing my own job and focus on driving fast.

"So I'm pleased that it can be something that can run very separately to me.

"We have great people running the whole thing, but I can also just be part of it when I'm able to. It's been great."

Helping drivers one-by-one

Alongside the racing team is the LN4 Legacy Programme that is more focused on picking out young drivers and taking them all the way to F1.

"The Legacy Programme is more to pick out individuals, people that I believe can get to F1, and we believe can get to F1, and try and help them one at a time," Norris said.

"That's our initial goal, when you say hundreds of thousands, you're still talking about millions of dollars to help one person.

"When you say to help a much bigger group, you're talking about needing a lot more money. We've got to start somewhere, and I'm happy that I'm trying to help at least one to begin with, and then we'll work on two, and then three, and then four, and five.

"But the bigger project is not just what one thing can one driver do? If you want to help bigger areas and economies that are just worse to start racing and allow people to start their dream, it's much bigger than just me doing my job and trying to help out on that.

"That takes the sport itself, that takes a lot more work from F1, from FIA, from karting companies. It's just simply too expensive, so you cannot rely on people just to fund more people. You have to find other ways to make it more friendly for people to start racing, especially financially.

"You've got to lower the costs somehow of teams, of the ability to go testing, of just signing up to do F2. F2 is over $2million, or €2m I think, to start. You've got to start somewhere.

"My ability is starting with one, and that's already a big project, and I think bigger than what people expect, but I want to expand on that. That takes time.

"Obviously, I have my own go-kart. I know other drivers, and Daniel [Ricciardo] and so forth have started projects to get more kids into racing. That's certainly my plan, but this is the beginning of it.

"With time and with more partners coming on board, and more money, more support, we can turn it into a way of helping more people from around the world."

Norris isn't the only one...

Plenty of drivers like Albon expressed an interest in doing something similar, but one driver is forming their own driver development project: Cadillac's Sergio Perez.

"It's really nice what Lando has done. From my side, I'm also at the point of my career that I would like to do something," Perez said.

"I'm preparing something with my manager, Khalil [Beschir], for the near term.

"We will be able to share that in the next few months - but we are definitely working on something from our side because we would like to give back to the sport and help the younger generations as well."

items.title: What's next for Aston Martin's and Honda's F1 development
items.author: Jack Cozens
items.content:
Aston Martin's major Hungarian Grand Prix upgrade package and subsequent refinements it introduced at the Dutch GP look set to be its final developments of the 2026 Formula 1 season.

Here are the main takeaways from that - as well as more on what engine partner Honda can do over the remainder of the year.

Aston Martin overhauled its car significantly at the Hungaroring before the summer break with the introduction of what essentially amounted to a B-spec car.

That 16-part upgrade package included a new, lighter chassis and a new front wing concept - adjustments to which were made after the summer break at Zandvoort, where Aston Martin also introduced revised floor fences and a modification to its diffuser winglet.

As a result, the team has introduced the joint-fourth-highest total of updates in 2026, with 34, though it jumps to second on the list - behind only Ferrari - when only performance updates are taken into account. The Race estimates it as being the highest upgrade spender so far this year.

Cardile stated, though, that the parts introduced recently would be "the last planned aero developments" for its 2026 car.

He said the only exception would be as a result of Aston Martin discovering something in its 2027 car development that "makes sense to test on track this year to help our correlation".

"But as of now, nothing more is scheduled," Cardile added.

Where more laptime can be found

What will still change in the coming month is the weight of the car.

Cardile confirmed Aston Martin still had "our weight‑saving programme to complete" and that it expects this to be done at the Azerbaijan GP, from which point "we'll essentially be running the final version of the car for the rest of the season".

While there has been no official word on how much Aston Martin is, or was, over the limit, the suggestion is that at its peak the initial version of the AMR26 was 10-15kg too heavy.

Cardile said Aston Martin would be "very, very close" to the weight limit by the time of the Baku race weekend on September 24-26.

"It depends on what you choose as your reference race, but it’s a significant number - enough to dramatically improve laptime," he said, when asked how much weight had been saved.

"That's a major achievement. Sometimes it comes from changing individual parts. Other times, it means rethinking how something was engineered in the first place - even the chassis. It's a mix of small details and big structural ideas."

Cardile said in reference to Aston Martin's recent uptick in performance that he had recognised the frustration felt by drivers Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll and said it was "important for us to get closer to giving them a car they can drive the way they want".

Having accomplished that - with Alonso scoring points for only the second time in 2026 with a season's-best ninth at Zandvoort - Cardile said: "Now though, a lot of the conversation with them is about looking ahead. We're asking: what are the limitations of the 2026 car, and how do we make sure we take another big step for 2027?"

But while saying the focus for the remainder of the campaign will be to use everything it can learn to "guide the 2027 project", he said there was no expectation that parts from this season would be used next year.

"Every single part will be new," he said. "Everything will have been improved.

"But conceptually, it will be an evolution of the direction we took with this year's car.

"We're on the right path now, but we’re not tied to it. Let's put it this way: when it comes to tackling the '27 project, we haven't placed any constraints on ourselves in terms of trying to carry anything over from the previous car.

"In this sense, it will be a completely new car, and it gives us the freedom and mindset to achieve what we want."

Honda brought its spec 2 engine upgrade to the Dutch GP - and this was an improvement. "We've made a double step, if you like: a big increase in raw performance and a big improvement in driveability," Cardile said.

He said at the Italian GP that another countermeasure to improve this would be introduced following work at Honda's Sakura facility.

But these kinds of updates are likely to be the extent of what Honda brings over the remainder of 2026.

Asked at Zandvoort whether any further hardware improvements were expected for this year, Orihara said: "This is the only major update for this year.

"But if we found something, a good solution to improve our performance by small modification, that can be on the table. But [there won't be] a major update before 2027."

Orihara nevertheless felt there was more power to be found - an estimate is that the Zandvoort upgrade provided a step in the 10-30bhp range - from optimisation.

"We have brought some calibration change for this track to maximise our performance, but it's going to be no big change, just optimisation," Orihara said at Monza, when asked by The Race whether more performance was available.

Alonso said the Honda upgrade was "not a big improvement, to be honest" - as he and Stroll were having difficulty exploiting the extra power - but asked by The Race if he still believed Honda could get back to the title-winning level it was at with Red Bull, he said: "100% yes. 100%.

"It's a huge commitment from Honda. The facilities we have in Japan are one of the best. I think the personnel and the management of the power unit now has been reinforced as Honda said - and all the people that were in the previous project, they are in again on this one, so I think I have no doubts and I trust 100% Honda.

"We just need to shortcut somehow that process."

items.title: Carlos Sainz becomes newest Giorgio Armani 'Fragrance Ambassador'
items.author: Hannah Atkinson
items.content:
Carlos Sainz is adding a stylish paragraph to his CV after being announced as the newest Giorgio Armani Spain Fragrance Ambassador for theI WILL Eau de Parfum. 

He is the latest face of Armani Beauty, with the brand saying Carlos represents “authentic elegance, fierce discipline” - and we have to agree. 

Carlos looked the part, too, during his latest visit to Venice, attending the Venice Film Festival, just before heading to Monza for the Italian GP this weekend.

Giorgio Armani dressed a group of their guests for opening night, including Sainz. He wore a Giorgio Armani tuxedo, which included an ivory dinner jacket, standing out among the sea of black tuxedos, and paired it with black trousers. He was joined on the red carpet by his partner Rebecca Donaldson. 

Between racing, red carpets and now a Giorgio Armani campaign, Carlos has really been keeping busy. We will be keeping an eye out for what stylish moment comes next!

items.title: A2RL's international racing debut: What you need to know
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
The most advanced autonomous racing series in the world has headed to Europe for the first time, with Imola hosting a race between five autonomous single-seaters this Saturday.

The Abu Dhabi Autonomous Racing League (A2RL) returns with its first major on-track event since staging its 2025 finale in Abu Dhabi last November, where teams competed for a $2.25million prize pool.

This time around, five teams have qualified for a race at Imola this Saturday, where they'll race Super Formula cars which have been heavily adapted to drive autonomously.

Here's everything you need to know about A2RL's international debut:

Teams are using the A2RL EAV-25 platform, which marks a huge step forward from the series' initial autonomous concept.

There's no better evidence for that than it lapping just 1.58 seconds off ex-F1 driver Daniil Kvyat at Abu Dhabi last November, having been 10 seconds adrift at Suzuka just 18 months prior to that.

"Still, today, after two and a half years here, I'm still amazed when I see this car running," A2RL technical director Nicola Palarchi told The Race at Imola.

"The level of performance when they approach, when they attack a corner is amazing.

"And thinking that there's no one there [in the cockpit], and it's not remote control...there's no predefined driving or strategies, the car is driving by itself and making its own decision, [is] mind-blowing."

Imola presents a huge, new challenge for the technology, with far more bumps and kerbs than Abu Dhabi, very little margin for error with gravel traps aplenty, and variable weather conditions.

So teams have been given nine days of testing at Imola prior to the Saturday finale. They all have identical EAV-25s and the autonomous stack that sits within the cockpit and has been developed by the series, but it's down to the teams to code their AI machines to be the fastest.

Teams qualified their cars at the end of those nine days of testing, with Italian outfit Unimore Racing coming out on top, ahead of fellow home team Polimove.

1m37.314s +1.084s +1.746s +2.936s +3.964s

Season one and two champion TUM was third, but it knows the result is far from settled.

That's because these autonomous cars really can race each other, with TUM passing Unimore for victory in the Abu Dhabi finale last year.

Just like in traditional motorsport, there are also trade-offs for the teams to make when programming the cars, in terms of one-lap speed and race pace, so there's every possibility that the order will change in Saturday's race.

The laptimes have been very competitive too. A2RL says the fastest time got to within eight and a half tenths of the benchmark human laptime, set by current Super Formula driver Juju Noda.

The cars have been weatherproofed

Presently, the weather forecast is for a scorchingly hot and dry Saturday at Imola. But should that change, A2RL is now ready for it.

A2RL's testing at Suzuka in 2024 exposed one vulnerability with the initial cars: in wet conditions, the sensors and autonomous stack were exposed to moisture, which caused some issues.

Therefore, a rainproofing kit can be fitted to the EAV-25, which means it can run in the wet - and has done successfully - at Imola. It even ran in hail conditions.

That kit includes sharkfin louvres on the cockpit to cover air exhaust vents, cockpit cover seals, and specifically designed and engineered rubber 3D-printed camera sleeves to seal the forward camera hatches.

"We are very happy; we have been working on a rain kit for some time," Palarchi told The Race.

"We had some rain already in 2024 when we were preparing for the exhibition in Suzuka at the time of the Super Formula event.

"We have been focusing on this in the last few months, as we knew we were coming to Imola and the weather is not as stable as in Abu Dhabi.

"So we managed to roll out the rain kit that was very successful, and the teams could enjoy wet track condition, which was a first also for all of them."

The five-car race will take place on Saturday, September 5 at 6.30pm local time.

items.title: Italian GP tipped for mad 'MotoGP-style' race with F1 2026 cars
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Formula 1 figures are bracing for the potential of a particularly wild Italian Grand Prix weekend at Monza, as slipstream is expected to massively impact both qualifying and the race.

Aston Martin trackside chief Mike Krack has forecast "a record of all times" in terms of overtaking in the grand prix, while 22-car Q1 - due to the massive benefit of towing and complexities of energy strategies - is particularly at risk of being dominated by the efforts to catch a slipstream.

F1 is heading to one of the most challenging venues for the new turbo hybrid 2026 cars, with Monza's long straights meaning cars are going to run out of battery energy easily.

Cars struggling for top speed on the straights, allied to the new active aero characteristics of straight and corner mode, means that there is now a much bigger benefit than there has been in recent years from receiving a tow.

Being in the slipstream of the car ahead will not only help increase top speed marginally by reducing drag, but will also deliver gains in terms of battery deployment - as less energy will need to be burned to push the car through the air.

Williams chief engineer Paul Williams reckons that slipstreaming could become a "significant tactic" once more. And Krack went as far as to express hope the gains do not trigger a repeat of what happened at Monza in 2019, when drivers tripped over themselves trying to get a slipstream at the end of qualifying.

Asked by The Race if slipstream games were back in play at Monza this year, having fallen away in recent years, Krack said: "I think yes!

"I think the lack of energy that you have here over the qualifying lap will manifest itself in people looking for that.

"I hope we will not have a situation like 2019, certainly not in Q1 - but who knows what will happen? Nobody wants to be first probably, but I think there will be more of this than we have seen here recently."

Cadillac driver Sergio Perez said of slipstreaming at Monza: "In previous generations it was [already] very critical.

"Now it's going to become even more, with the lack of energy that we're going to experience.

"We saw already in Spa it was around two seconds to a second and a half, so I think it's going to be really close.

"It's going to be a bit messy [in qualifying] because everyone will be trying to get some towing."

Measures are in place in modern F1 after the chaos of 2019 that should mitigate the issue, as the FIA has instituted a minimum laptime delta - but it's exceedingly rare for this to lead to a driver penalty, and the FIA may have to be stricter with enforcement this year than is convention.

One question that will only be answered when cars are running together is whether excessive slipstreaming could prompt some safety concerns.

This could become an issue if there are wildly different deployment strategies in play that mean there are big speed differentials between cars in areas of the track.

Krack said: "Normally if you see the deployment profiles, they converge over a weekend - so I do not expect any major differences.

"But if people deploy completely differently, then there is always a risk."

F1 teams know that this weekend is going to be incredibly challenging from an energy management perspective and that some unusual tactics may need to come out.

Krack felt that the new rules will force a completely different approach for teams.

"Monza is a bit of a new game this year that we need to learn how to handle," he said.

"I think all the teams will have to learn and maybe what we know about Monza is not necessarily true anymore."

One of the main uncertainties for qualifying will be how best to unleash energy coming out of the final Alboreto or Parabolica corner for the start of a qualifying lap.

Teams will have to work out where the best place is to go on full power to maximise speed for the start of the lap, but without burning up so much battery that they run short before the first chicane.

Despite the FIA's measures to combat these issues of energy starvation, Perez said: "You're going to get into this situation where if you went half a percent too much in one corner on throttle, it's going to cost you even a few tenths.

"Belgium [Spa-Francorchamps] was very critical in that regard and I expect that here it's going to be, like, the worst of them all."

Krack suggested Monza could produce an extreme level of yo-yo racing.

He said it remained unclear how easy overtaking would be, but expected it will "probably will be a record of all times here, or like MotoGP".

Though Monza's layout should naturally lead itself to this kind of racing, that hasn't really been the case in F1 in recent years - with the venue struggling to deliver much in the way of wheel-to-wheel action, though Formula 2 and Formula 3 have remained "overtake-fests".

This time, the expectation is of a grand prix more in line with those kinds of categories.

"Top speeds are way down from the past - which is a bit of a shame, but on certain straights you can make a bigger difference than before when it comes to defending or attacking," said Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas.

"It's been normally a good place for racing anyway but now it adds another element of more dynamic racing here. So no doubt there's going to be plenty of overtakes."

Rookie Arvid Lindblad was more pessimistic, though, after what he described as "the most confusing sim session of the year" in preparation for Monza's unique energy challenges.

"I think the first two laps will be interesting, depending where you spend your energy you'll pass three cars and then lose to three cars," he said. "[After that] I don't know if there's going to be much passing.

"I think the difference to other tracks, even energy-starved ones, if you use the boost it takes you one lap to recover, so you're a bit slow on the next two or three straights, but one lap after you're alright, whereas here it takes a lot longer to recover. So basically if you use the boost, you gain on one straight, but then you're so slow for the next three laps.

"So I think it will... you could call it 'yo-yo racing' maybe, but I just think it will be really bad yo-yo racing. Even in the past it used to be decent, we would actually be passing each other, whereas now it's just, you're going to pass the guy and then you're just going to lose a second and a half. I don't know what to expect, but I'm not very optimistic."

items.title: F1's take on its battle to satisfy new and old fans
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Bernie Ecclestone once infamously said that there was little point in Formula 1 chasing a younger audience, because they could not afford what sponsors had on offer.

Now, well into the post-Ecclestone Liberty Media era, F1 not only has a bigger audience but a much younger one, too.

The latest figures issued by F1 suggest that 830 million people now follow grand prix racing, which is 64% up from 2018 when its current owner took over.

It is estimated that 43% of F1's audience is now under 35, with 42% of the audience female. Out of the new fans, three quarters are female.

While the numbers are a huge triumph for Liberty, they are also at the heart of a debate triggered by the divided opinion over the 2026 rules.

How much should F1 and its stakeholders obsess over the new audience, and what should you do about the fans who have long been there?

Turn off the hardcore, who will stick with you through thick and thin, then there may be nobody left if the bubble bursts and the casuals are lost, too.

Those notorious Ecclestone remarks about younger fans came just as F1 began its hybrid era back in 2014.

"Young kids will see the Rolex brand, but are they going to go and buy one?" he said back then. "They can't afford it. Or our other sponsor, UBS - these kids don't care about banking. They haven't got enough money to put in the bloody banks anyway. That's what I think."

F1 is in a very different place right now, thanks to the new approach taken by Liberty.

According to FOM's chief communications and corporate relations officer Liam Parker, this wasn't an Americanisation of F1.

"It was a modernisation approach," he told The Race.

There was a time in the 1980s when all F1 had to really care about was making sure it was in front of as many TV eyeballs as possible on Sunday afternoons.

Ecclestone's approach to maximise the audience and the value for broadcast deals was to lock down the distribution of content to increase its exclusivity.

His successors – then-CEO Chase Carey and commercial chief Sean Bratches – viewed things differently. Rather than shut off everything on social media and view it as the enemy, they embraced it and saw opportunity.

Parker says: "Their view was, 'well, look, we've got access to all of this. How can we cut this in different ways?'.

"'Why don't we have a social media team that is large enough to service a wider audience? Why are the teams not allowed to post content? Why are the drivers not allowed?'"

It was this mindset that opened the doors for a different approach through social media and paved the way for the Netflix: Drive to Survive show that had a major role in delivering a new audience.

While Drive to Survive was important in attracting a new F1 audience, it should not be viewed as the magic bullet that did it all. Instead, it more amplified F1's new Liberty Media approach.

Parker adds: "A lot of credit is given to Netflix about what it did, and it deserves it, but it wasn't the panacea.

"I genuinely believe the opening up of social media access, alongside the Netflix environment, that then built into the F1 film and other things, shifted the demographic quite substantially. That's taken time."

What a new audience means

When audiences and customers change, organisations must react.

There is always a balancing act required in responding to what your new followers want without it risking being a turn-off for those who have been around a while.

In F1's case, it has been able to satisfy different segments quite easily off track by simply expanding the content on offer.

There are those happy to follow F1 simply through watching 15-second TikTok videos, while those that want technical analyses that pore over the finest of details can find that, too. One offering does not come at the expense of the other.

As Parker says: "If you just rely on, ‘let's just put out racing content', you're serving a certain market and hoping that the new market will just like that.

"You've got to keep up with trends. You've got to work out where the trends are.

"There's no point saying, ‘OK, we've got a growing fanbase aged between 16 and 20,' without saying, ‘well, what do they consume? How do they get their information? How do they get their entertainment? What news do they consume? What are they interested in and what are they not interested in?'"

It is here where F1 faces a bit of a juggling act because different audiences value different content in different ways.

For some, Lewis Hamilton's latest clothing choice is as important as the latest rear wing design is to others.

"If you talk about tyres and degradation in a video, then there's a whole load of people that just don't understand it," adds Parker. "They perhaps feel stupid and then don't want to be a part of it.

"They just want to know that Charles Leclerc turned up with the dog today. How big is George Russell's fiancée's wedding ring?

"That is just different content. What we shouldn't say is 'this [bit of content is] trivial, and that bit is far more serious'."

The hardcore vs casual debate

Varying needs of different audience segments go beyond just content though, because the make-up of the fanbase inevitably feeds through to what shape F1 itself should take.

When it comes to deciding rule changes, a key factor is always whether fans will like them or they'll prove to be a turn-off. And you are never going to please all the fans all the time.

There are times when a series has to decide whether it moulds itself into becoming what its fanbase wants, or if it commits to doing what it thinks is best and expects the audience to adapt.

This is something that F1 has faced head-on in 2026 with the new regulations having clearly divided opinion between audience segments.

Some have embraced the action-packed overtakes that many F1 drivers and hardcore fans have bemoaned as fake. Many could also not care less about the cars being energy-starved and how super-clipping has ruined some great corners.

F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali recently caused some controversy as he upset established and new fans alike in response to a question about the more hardcore of followers not liking the new rules.

"There are diehard motorsport fans who talk about clipping during a Formula 1 weekend," he told De Telegraaf. "But there will also be many who think of a clip as something you put in your hair."

Coming off the back of a comment he made over the summer that "no one is interested in how you drive the car", Domenicali's stance has left many long-term fans questioning whether they are now just a minority that F1 no longer cares about.

Parker is clear that is not the case - and he suggests Domenicali's hair clip remark was misinterpreted.

"I was in the room, and Stefano wasn't dismissive," he said. "He explained that he was a super fan, but he also had to think about those that are not.

"There's a great set of people out there that are our core, that care about clipping and battery state and charge, and you must give them that content.

"But there's others out there that think a clip is what you put in your hair. He wasn't saying that no one cares about super clipping. It's just different content ignites different people in different debates."

Not messing with the rules

Parker is adamant that while F1 has not hesitated to rip things up when it comes to content, there is a red line that it will not cross.

It is that grand prix racing must remain a meritocracy where the best drivers in the best cars come out on top. The sport will always come before the entertainment.

"The sport is the core," he said. "You can't mess with that."

Parker says evidence of this being central to Liberty's remit is that, while it's not afraid to shake up the experience for fans at grand prix weekends, the on-track elements have not been radically overhauled.

"I bet if you went back 10 years and asked someone to crystal ball gaze and say, ‘what do you think Liberty as an American company would do to F1', you'd say 'they will probably have sprinklers and have fake this and fake that'," he said.

"I think the most ambitious thing we've really done on track is to evolve the sprint races over time."

For F1, delivering a quality spectacle that stays true to its roots is something that is good for all fans.

"If that's strong, then everything else has a strong basis," added Parker.

"If people are saying that racing is rubbish, the drivers are boring, there's no entertainment, these cars are not interesting, then there isn't a Netflix story, there isn't a social media story."

But he says that F1 must be mindful that it cannot stay locked in the past. It has to evolve and adapt to ensure that there is a new generation of fans coming through, otherwise global interest will fall away.

"If F1 works and is fundamentally strong, then everything else goes from it," he said.

"There are fans that have been with us a long time, and they are vital. Hopefully they will be with us all the way through.

"But we would be wrong to say that, as a sport, all these other people that don't understand the technology, 'we don't want you'. From a sporting perspective and potentially a commercial perspective it would be stupid.

"I know sometimes it gets lost in understanding, but Stefano has been in the sport for 30 years, it's his business, but he's got to think: 'How do I make it bigger? How do I grow?'

"Because if you sit still, the NBA, cricket, football, everything else will grow, and we'll be left behind."

Sitting still is not something you'd associate with the Liberty F1 era, but keeping that much more varied audience  – rather than winning it over in the first place – could be its greatest challenge yet.

items.title: Norris sets up racing team with ex-Prema chief
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Lando Norris has co-founded a new racing team – LN4 Fusion – and launched a driver development programme as part of a two-pronged effort to help young driving talent on the way towards Formula 1.

LN4 Fusion, which has pulled together a host of top-class talent from motorsport including the highly-respected Rene Rosin as its team principal, is to compete in the Italian F4 championship, the FIA Formula Regional European Championship and F3 next season.

It has sights set on joining F2, and has already begun a British F4 testing programme as it aims to secure an entry to that category.

As well as the racing team, Norris has also launched the LN4 Legacy Programme. This is a fully funded young driver scheme, which will be led by former Alpine sporting director Julian Rouse.

Speaking about the decision to commit to both projects, Norris said that he wanted to “create opportunities for the next generation, both on and off the track, and hopefully make a real difference to young drivers coming through the sport”.

With his own path to F1 being helped by backing from his family and then the support of McLaren, Norris is well aware that being fast is not all that is needed to succeed.

“I’ve been really lucky to have some amazing people around me throughout my career, and I know that getting to Formula 1 takes so much more than just talent,” he said.

“You need the right people around you, the right support and the right opportunities at the right time. That’s what these two projects are all about.

“LN4 Fusion is about building a race team that can compete with the best in junior motorsport, with great people and a great environment for drivers to develop. The LN4 Legacy Programme is about helping talented young drivers get opportunities they might not otherwise have.”

LN4 Fusion has the backing of an investment group that is led by Dan Richards, and has acquired selected assets from the AIX Racing operation, which has a licence to race in F3 until the end of 2027. It has also begun the application process to join F2.

Rosin’s signing is a coup as the Italian, who has won more than 40 junior championships at various levels, has been pondering his next steps following his surprise exit from Prema earlier this year. Another long-time Prema figure, engineer Guillaume Capietto, has also joined LN4 Fusion.

The team's European headquarters will be in Veneto in northern Italy where a new facility is being built. There will also be a British operation based in Cambridgeshire, that will be run by Dan Hazlewood, who has led the successful Fusion Motorsport karting team to multiple national and international titles in recent years.

Richards, who is CEO of LN4 Fusion, believed that getting a roster of world-class talent on board was critical to making a success of the operation.

"It has taken an enormous collective effort to bring the different elements together, but the objective from the beginning has been to build this properly and for the long term,” he said.

Norris’s plans have received the backing of F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali, who says his involvement will help further cement the strength of F1's support series.

“Seeing Lando Norris involved in this new project is an incredible statement on how much the pyramid of Formula 3 and Formula 2 is crucial to the future of Formula 1,” he said.

“Through Lando’s investment and experience, we can build a future, with new drivers, engineers, mechanics, and a tradition that will be followed by motorsport lovers.”

items.title: MotoGP 2027 testing: Dates and tracks announced
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
MotoGP factories have been intensively testing their 2027 prototypes all through this year - but full-grid testing will only commence once the 2026 season has concluded.

The usual one-day test in Valencia on the Tuesday after this year's season finale will be followed two months later by a two-day shakedown and two-day test at Sepang, and a two-day test at Buriram.

Most of the grid will thus get five days of pre-season 850cc running with Pirelli tyres.

Rookies will be an exception, allowed to run in the shakedown along with the factories' test riders. While this is totally normal practice for MotoGP, it could be more contentious than usual this year - as some believe next year's rookies (coming from Moto2 or World Superbikes) already have a built-in advantage in their knowledge of Pirelli rubber from their respective series'.

- Dec 1 (Tue) - Jan 29 (Fri) and Jan 30 (Sat)- Jan 31 (Sun) and Feb 1 (Mon) - Feb 6 (Sat) and Feb 7 (Sun)

There will be a gap of a month between the Buriram test and the season-opening Thai Grand Prix at the same venue.

items.title: Lawson gets another Red Bull outing with Hadjar sidelined again
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Red Bull Formula 1 driver Isack Hadjar will remain on the sidelines for the Italian Grand Prix at Monza, with Liam Lawson continuing to deputise.

Hadjar, who was absent from the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort due to a wrist fracture, is known to be taking a cautious approach to his recovery - having sought advice from MotoGP legend Marc Marquez, who endured career-changing complications after trying to return too soon from an arm break in 2020.

Red Bull said it is "closely monitoring" Hadjar's rehabilitation and that, despite "encouraging progress", it "will take no unnecessary risks with his return".

"It's good to hear Isack is recovering well and is back in the car soon, but it's great to have another weekend with the team," said Lawson, who was reasonably competitive on his first outing in the RB22 at Zandvoort, placing seventh in the grand prix.

"Zandvoort gave me a really useful first reference in the car, and having a full sprint weekend behind me means I'm coming into Monza with a much better understanding of the car and what I need from it."

Lawson will drive the full weekend schedule, while Max Verstappen will cede his RB22 to Ayumu Iwasa as part of the season-long obligation to tick off four rookie practice outings.

Like at Zandvoort, Yuki Tsunoda will replace Lawson in his usual Racing Bulls car.

items.title: Gilles Villeneuve biopic to premiere at Toronto film festival
items.author: Fleur Mealing
items.content:
A feature-length biopic charting the early life of Formula 1 legend Gilles Villeneuve will make its world premiere later this month, before a wider theatrical release in 2027.

Villeneuve: Rise of a Legend will close the Toronto International Film Festival on September 19, with a Quebec cinema release scheduled for November and a global launch planned for early next year.

The timing coincides with the 50th anniversary of Villeneuve's F1 debut at the 1977 British Grand Prix.

The French-language film focuses on Villeneuve's formative years in Quebec, tracing his rise from snowmobile racer to Formula Atlantic star and eventual F1 prospect.

Québécois actor Rémi Goulet plays Villeneuve, while director Yan Lanouette Turgeon said the project has been more than a decade in development.

"For me, Gilles Villeneuve's story needed to be told," said Turgeon. "He was such an interesting character. He remains a monumental figure in Quebec and in Formula 1, and a movie had never been made about him.

"I felt I needed to be the one to make this movie, and the timing is perfect as interest in Formula 1 has never been greater."

Villeneuve's son Jacques, the 1997 F1 world champion, said he was particularly pleased that the film explores a period of his father's life that has largely remained out of the public eye.

"Watching the trailer, it was difficult to hold back the tears. And I love that it focuses on the early years, the years no one but our family knows about," Jacques Villeneuve said.

"Most biopics focus on when someone's in their prime. They give the audience what they already know, whereas this film shows the building blocks."

The film revisits Villeneuve's upbringing in rural Quebec, his emergence as one of North America's leading snowmobile racers and his success in Formula Atlantic competition.

It also depicts the pivotal 1976 Formula Atlantic race at Trois-Rivières, where Villeneuve defeated several established F1 drivers, including that year's eventual F1 world champion James Hunt, helping to put Villeneuve on the radar of grand prix teams.

Production included filming at Montreal's Circuit Gilles-Villeneuve, which was renamed in his honour following his death in 1982. Replica period racing machinery was supplied by Race Car Replicas, the company behind the cars used in the film .

The project has involved Villeneuve's family throughout its development, with daughter Melanie Villeneuve serving as an executive producer.

"When I started on this journey, I wanted to understand my father's public legacy and reclaim our family heritage," she said.

"I wanted to ensure his memory was preserved by those who loved him most.

"The film charts the incredible rise of a working-class man from rural Quebec who became Enzo Ferrari's favourite driver."

items.title: Miami GP changes title sponsor
items.author: Samarth Kanal
items.content:
The Formula 1 Miami Grand Prix will from 2027 be sponsored by Hard Rock, which has held the naming rights to the NFL’s Miami Dolphins stadium since 2016.

The Miami GP - which previously had Crypto.com as its title sponsor - is contracted to remain on the F1 calendar through to 2041.

This new title sponsor agreement will see Hard Rock branding incorporated into the official event title - making it the Formula 1 Hard Rock Miami Grand Prix - along with track, paddock, fan area, and podium signage.

Hard Rock will continue its deal to produce live entertainment at the track.

The 2026 iteration of the Miami GP included performances by Nelly, Zedd, Marshmello, Kane Brown and others.

“Hard Rock has been part of Miami’s Formula 1 story from the very beginning, and we are incredibly proud to welcome them as the new title partner of the Formula 1 Hard Rock Miami Grand Prix,” said Miami GP president Katharina Nowak.

“This partnership marks a new era for our race, as we look to build upon the success of our first five years and continue to evolve alongside one of the most iconic and culturally significant brands in the world in Hard Rock.”

Hard Rock already sponsors the Beach Club hospitality area that is located on the outside of Turns 11 to 13 of the Miami International Autodrome. This area will be revamped for 2027 - with ticket-holders able to experience live performances, cabanas with views of the track and food and beverage options.

“They [Hard Rock] have been alongside us in growing Hard Rock Stadium into a global sports and entertainment destination for more than a decade and in establishing our race as one of the defining moments on the Formula 1 calendar,” added Nowak. 

“Together, we will seek to set a new standard of what is possible when the best of racing, entertainment and culture converge in Miami, and we could not be more excited for this new chapter together.”

Hard Rock’s chairman Jim Allen added that the “partnership reflects Hard Rock’s commitment to delivering world-class experiences to international audiences.”

Hard Rock International is a privately-held company owned by the Seminole Tribe of Florida, which purchased it for $965 million USD in 2007. It owns more than 300 restaurants and cafes, and more than 80 hotels and casinos around the world.

items.title: Free McLaren F1 showrun announced for Athens
items.author: Fleur Mealing
items.content:
McLaren Racing and partner Allwyn will bring a Formula 1 showrun to Athens on October 3 as part of a new global fan event series.

The free event, called Allwyn x McLaren Racing: Live in Athens, will take place outside the Olympic Athletic Center of Athens (OAKA) in Greece.

Fans will be able to see McLaren's 2025 F1 World constructors' championship-winning car in action, alongside Ayrton Senna's McLaren MP4/6. Two-time F1 world champion Mika Häkkinen will also drive during the event.

Other former F1 drivers and personalities are expected to attend - however, who it will be exactly is yet to be confirmed. Additional modern and historic McLaren cars will be displayed at the event alongside a fan zone and other entertainment activities.

Athens will be the first stop in a new series of fan events being launched by Allwyn and McLaren Racing. 

"Launching this global event series in Athens is a major milestone for our partnership with McLaren Racing," said Pavel Turek, Allwyn's chief officer of global partnerships.

"Bringing more speed, thrills and excitement to this iconic sporting location is the perfect way to introduce our international event platform and entertain more fans around the world."

Allwyn Hellas chairman and CEO Jan Karas said the event would be one of the largest motorsport fan experiences ever held in Greece.

"We're expecting to welcome thousands of fans in October, which will make Allwyn x McLaren Racing: Live in Athens one of the largest motorsport fan experiences ever held in Greece," he said.

McLaren Racing chief marketing officer Louise McEwen said the event was designed to help bring the team closer to fans who are unable to attend Formula 1 races.

"Our fans are at the heart of everything we do at McLaren Racing, and while not everyone can experience a Grand Prix weekend in person, we're always looking for ways to bring the team closer to them," she said.

The event will be free to attend, with no ticket needed. Further details on appearances, experiences and event activities will be announced ahead of the October event on Allwyn and McLaren’s social media.
